bib.title: Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis
bib.venue: inferred: Springer chapter (DOI 10.1007/11681878_14) and file name give 2006; the PDF text prints no venue or year

question: How much noise must be added to a query answer to keep a statistical database private, for general (not just sum) query functions?
hypothesis: Noise calibrated to the sensitivity of the query (largest change one row can cause), not to the database size or output dimension, suffices for privacy.
contributions: Define epsilon-indistinguishability of transcripts as the privacy notion and show equivalence to simulatability and semantic-security formulations
Define L1 sensitivity and prove Laplace noise Lap(S(f)/eps) gives eps-indistinguishability, including for adaptive query sequences
Sensitivity analyses of histograms, contingency tables, covariance matrices, distance-from-a-property and sample-approximable functions
Separation: non-interactive mechanisms need databases of size 2^Omega(d) to answer all low-sensitivity sum queries; interactive mechanisms do not

results.claim: Laplace noise with scale S(f)/epsilon added independently to each of d coordinates of f(x) is epsilon-indistinguishable, for every f: D^n -> R^d (Proposition 1, non-interactive output perturbation).
results.setup: Any f with finite L1 sensitivity; database of n rows over domain D; neighbours differ in one entry; noise i.i.d. Lap(S(f)/eps); a theorem, no experiment.

results.claim: Adaptive version (Theorem 1): if lambda = max_t S(f_t)/epsilon, answering each adaptively chosen query f_i(x)+Lap(lambda) is epsilon-indistinguishable for an arbitrary adversary; the server may refuse queries whose S(f_t) is above a threshold.
results.setup: Transcript t = answers a_1..a_d; f_t's i-th coordinate depends on first i-1 answers; privacy budget epsilon is spent across the whole transcript by max_t S(f_t), not per query.

results.claim: Definition 1 bounds the absolute log-ratio of transcript probabilities by epsilon for all neighbouring databases, all adversaries and all transcripts.
results.setup: Databases are vectors in D^n; neighbours differ in exactly one entry (Hamming distance 1).

results.claim: Histogram L1 sensitivity is 2, independent of the number of bins d.
results.setup: Histogram over d disjoint bins; changing one row moves one point between two bins.
results.quote:
The L1 sensitivity of f is thus 2,
independent of d.

results.claim: Noisy sum of 0/1 entries needs Lap(1/epsilon); sensitivity 1.
results.setup: x in {0,1}^n, f(x)=sum x_i, Y ~ Lap(1/eps).

results.claim: Mean of v(x_i) with bound gamma = max ||v(x)||_1 changes by at most 2*gamma/n in L1 when one row changes; covariance matrix changes by at most 8*gamma^2/n.
results.setup: mu = avg v(x_i), C = avg v v^T - mu mu^T; gamma bounds the L1 norm of v; matrix L1 norm treated as d^2-dimensional vector.
results.quote: results in a vector µ+δ where ∥δ∥1 ≤2γ/n

results.claim: Distance from any set S (Hamming distance to nearest point in S) has sensitivity 1; min-cut weight and minimum spanning tree weight (edge weights in [0,1]) are 1-sensitive.
results.setup: Databases of n entries; for a graph, entries are edge weights on m vertices with n = C(m,2).

results.claim: Lemma 1: if a randomized algorithm reads each x_i with probability at most alpha and is within L1 distance sigma of f(x) with probability at least beta = (1+alpha)/2, then S(f) <= 2 sigma. Converse fails (Reed-Solomon codeword distance has sensitivity 1 but needs about k queries).

Theorem 2: in a metric output space where h_{f(x),eps}(y) proportional to exp(eps*d_M(y,z)/(2 S_M(f))) is well-defined (normalisable), sampling per Eqn 4 is epsilon-indistinguishable (an early exponential-mechanism form).
results.setup: Needs metric d_M (symmetry, triangle inequality) and a finite normaliser; factor 2 can be dropped when the normaliser does not depend on z (Remark 1).

results.claim: Theorem 3: for any non-interactive epsilon-indistinguishable mechanism with domain {0,1}^d, for at least 2/3 of parity-type sum queries f_g, the two transcript distributions (all g=0 vs all g=n) have statistical difference O(n^{4/3} eps^{2/3} 2^{-d/3}); so the database needs 2^{Omega(d)} rows, i.e. n = o(2^{d/4}/sqrt(eps)) is not enough.
results.setup: Non-interactive sanitisation; g_r(i,x)= r_i inner product x mod 2, r_i non-zero; quantifier order matters (a single query can be answered by a tailored scheme).

results.claim: Proposition 2: for randomized response schemes the bound tightens to statistical difference O(n eps^{2/3} 2^{-d/3}); needs n = o(2^{d/3}/eps^{2/3}).
results.setup: Each row perturbed individually by Z; same predicate on all rows; at least 2/3 of r in {0,1}^d \ {0^d}.

results.claim: Histogram noise: earlier SuLQ framework adds O(sqrt(d)/eps) per coordinate, giving total L1 error a factor O(sqrt(d)) larger than the sensitivity-based scheme; covariance matrix a factor O(d) larger.
results.setup: Comparison with Blum, Dwork, McSherry, Nissim 2005 (SuLQ).

results.claim: Group privacy: a (1, eps/k)-indistinguishable mechanism is (k, eps)-indistinguishable.
results.setup: Chain argument over k single-entry changes.

results.claim: Nonnegligible leakage is inherent: to get even a constant-factor approximation of a count, eps must be Omega(1/n).

limits: Theory only: no experiments, no empirical utility numbers or datasets.
Assumes a trusted server holding the database; neighbours differ in exactly one entry (Hamming distance 1).
epsilon is a policy choice with no guidance on its value; utility needs epsilon of order 1/n or larger for counts.

The Laplace density is described as having standard deviation lambda; the standard deviation of Lap(lambda) is sqrt(2)*lambda (the paper's statement is imprecise; the privacy proof uses only the scale).
Theorem 1 requires a bound lambda = max_t S(f_t)/eps over all transcripts, so S must be known and bounded before answering.
Definition has no delta term (pure epsilon only); the later (epsilon, delta) relaxation is not in this paper.
Separation result applies to non-interactive mechanisms satisfying Definition 1; the paper notes (footnote 4) it fails under weaker definitions.
Theorem 2 only applies when the density normalises to a finite integral.

terms.definition: A mechanism is epsilon-indistinguishable if for all pairs x, x' in D^n which differ in only one entry, for all adversaries A, and for all transcripts t: |ln(Pr[T_A(x)=t]/Pr[T_A(x')=t])| <= epsilon.
The smallest number S(f) such that for all x, x' in D^n which differ in a single entry, ||f(x)-f(x')||_1 <= S(f).
Density h(y) proportional to exp(-|y|/lambda), mean 0 (paper says standard deviation lambda).
S_M(f) = sup over x,x' with d_H(x,x')=1 of d_M(f(x), f(x')).
For every adversary A and every set I of size n-k there is an informed adversary A' such that |ln(Pr[T_{San,A}(x)=t]/Pr[A'(x|_I)=t])| <= eps for any x.
Every interaction with an informed adversary results in a bounded (by eps) change in the a-posteriori probability of any predicate.
An adversary who knows some set of n-k database entries before interacting with the mechanism.
